Dans La Clef des Songes ou dialogue avec le bon Dieu (1987) et d’autres textes littéraires comme Éloge de l’Inceste^{[3]} (1979) ou Développements sur la lettre de la Bonne Nouvelle (1990), il mêle sciences, métaphysique, mysticisme et religions, proposant une vision globale du monde.
# Présentation

Ce site contient les archives mathématiques d’Alexandre Grothendieck de 1949 à 1991. On y trouvera des manuscrits, des « tapuscrits », parfois des documents imprimés, dans un classement fidèle pour l’essentiel (quand il existait ) au classement de l’auteur. Sur les 28000 (environ) pages de ce fonds, seules 18000 (environ) sont actuellement accessibles : pour des raisons de droits on ne peut diffuser les lettres des correspondants de Grothendieck sans leur autorisation.

publicação da revista, resultante de proposta junto ao Conselho Deliberativo de Lelio

Gama, que, então, era membro do Instituto. Em 1946, a Diretoria do IBECC promovera

quatro prêmios, a saber, Prêmio de Educação, Prêmio de Ciência, Prêmio de Literatura e

Prêmio de Arte, no valor de Cr$ 50 mil cada um.

Manuel Bandeira, o Prêmio de Literatura, e Heitor Villa-Lobos, o Prêmio de Arte. A

Comissão de Ciências foi a única a não apresentar parecer no prazo estipulado, de modo

que a Diretoria resolveu designar a importância correspondente ao Prêmio de Ciência às

publicações em matemática realizadas por Lelio Gama. No período de 1947 a 1951, com

o apoio do IBECC, foi publicado o volume 2 da Summa Brasiliensis Mathematicae,

reunindo 10 fascículos. A luta na Faculdade Nacional de Filosofia para o desenvolvimento

L0@P0: Chapter 3. From student to celebrity: 1949-1952
L1@P0: The challenge of adequately describing the years that Alexandre Grothendieck spent
L2@P0: as a doctoral student in Nancy is considerable, for during those three years he underwent
L3@P0: some of the most tremendous experiences that life can bring to a young man, while simultaneously making a series of extraordinary mathematical discoveries: thus, the time
L4@P0: has come to weave a real, albeit informal, discussion of mathematics into the fabric tale of
L5@P0: Grothendieck’s life.
L6@P0: In terms of his previous education and reputation, Grothendieck was infinitely removed
L7@P0: from the family of young French talents so close to him in age, Ecole Normale students
L8@P0: spotted early on and nurtured all along their way to success: Pierre Samuel, Roger Godement, Ren´e Thom, Jacques Dixmier, Jean Cerf, Yvonne Bruhat and her brother Fran¸cois,
L9@P0: Jean-Pierre Serre, Bernard Malgrange. He was so completely unknown to this group and
L10@P0: to their professors, came from such a deprived and chaotic background, and was, compared to them, so ignorant at the start of his research career, that his fulgurating ascent
L11@P0: to sudden stardom is all the more incredible; quite unique in the history of mathematics.
L12@P0: Two startled professors: Fall 1949
L13@P0: An anecdote survives about Grothendieck’s arrival in Nancy: the story of his rude
L14@P0: reception at the hands of Dieudonn´e when, on their very first contact, he showed him a
L15@P0: dense handwritten manuscript on “generalized integrals”. He had already mentioned this
L16@P0: work in writing to Dieudonn´e, and had received a warm and friendly response in which
L17@P0: Dieudonn´e praised his “ardor for mathematics”. But Dieudonn´e’s initial receptiveness
L18@P0: did not outlast a first look at the actual text. Those who recall this incident (or rather,
L19@P0: who recall Dieudonn´e’s telling them about it) claim that Dieudonn´e gave Grothendieck a
L20@P0: rather sharp dressing down, finding that the work displayed a reprehensible tendency to
L21@P0: gratuitous generality. Whether or not his assessment is justifiable, it is clear in any case
L22@P0: that he immediately seized the essence of Grothendieck’s approach – and was quick to
L23@P0: discourage it. As Schwartz recounts it in his autobiography:
L24@P0: Il pr´esenta d’abord `a Dieudonn´e un article d’une cinquantaine de pages, sur “L’int´egration `a valeurs dans un groupe topologique”. C’´etait exact, mais rigoureusement sans
L25@P0: aucun int´erˆet. Dieudonn´e, avec l’agressivit´e (toujours passag`ere) dont il ´etait capable, lui
L26@P0: passa un savon m´emorable, arguant qu’on ne devait pas travailler de cette mani`ere, en
L27@P0: g´en´eralisant pour le plaisir de g´en´eraliser. Il fallait que le probl`eme trait´e soit difficile,
L28@P0: et susceptible d’applications dans le reste des math´ematiques (ou d’autres sciences); ses
L29@P0: r´esultats ne serviraient jamais `a rien ni `a personne. [Sch 292]1
L30@P0: The irrepressible Grothendieck does not seem to have conceived the slightest grudge
L31@P0: towards Dieudonn´e on this account; perhaps his own family experiences with aggressivity
L32@P0: and anger made him dismiss such scenes easily, or perhaps the scolding tone was not
L33@P0: enough to mask the underlying warm generosity and benevolence that Dieudonn´e was
L34@P0-1: 1noted for, as much or more than for his brusque manner and frequent loud explosions of
L35@P1: temper. Quite probably, Grothendieck simply accepted the rebuke as valid, cast aside his
L36@P1: past work without a thought as he had already done twice before, and rolled up his sleeves
L37@P1: to have a new stab at proving his worth, by working for the first time on problems set to
L38@P1: him by someone else.
L39@P1: In order to direct the young neophyte towards more concrete questions, Dieudonn´e
L40@P1: and Schwartz handed him a copy of their most recent paper∗, La dualit´e dans les espaces
L41@P1: F et LF. This article was an attempt to transport some major results in the theory of
L42@P1: Banach spaces (relations between different topologies and elements of the duality theory)
L43@P1: to more general locally convex topological vector spaces, essentially for the purpose of
L44@P1: developing Schwartz’s recent and exciting theory of distributions, for which he would win
L45@P1: the Fields Medal the following summer.
L46@P1: Interestingly, one of the new features of the Schwartz-Dieudonn´e article was the fact
L47@P1: that they built their (LF)-spaces by taking inductive limits of (F)-spaces. At that time,
L48@P1: the ideas of projective and inductive limits were relatively new; projective limits were used
L49@P1: in specific situations for specific constructions, without recourse to a general definition,
L50@P1: while inductive limits had, seemingly, only just made their first appearance, without yet
L51@P1: being recognized as a general procedure (and even less as the dual procedure to projective
L52@P1: limits), for the purpose of defining a topology on the space D of C
L53@P1: ∞ functions with compact
L54@P1: support studied by Schwartz. Later, Grothendieck and others would adopt and formalize
L55@P1: the definitions of these limits, essentially in the context of homological algebra, thus making
L56@P1: them into concepts uniformly applicable to a great many different mathematical situations
L57@P1: rather than just tools used once at a time in each context. This is just one of the features
L58@P1: of his early work in functional analysis which connects it in a deep way to his later body
L59@P1: of work. Because he left the subject of topological vector spaces in 1955 completely and
L60@P1: forever, it is often considered as something of a separate episode in his mathematical
L61@P1: life. But in fact, many of the mathematical seeds of his later work were sown during
L62@P1: his functional analysis period, and what is more, many of the traits that later came to
L63@P1: characterize his inimitable style were already present there as well. We will explore some
L64@P1: of these in more detail below.
L65@P1: The Dieudonn´e-Schwartz article ended with fourteen questions that the authors had
L66@P1: not been able to solve, all concerning desirable basic properties of (F)-spaces, their duals,
L67@P1: their topologies, their subsets, and the linear functionals on them. Dieudonn´e handed the
L68@P1: article to Grothendieck with the injunction to choose a few and think about them. As
L69@P1: Schwartz recounts it, Grothendieck disappeared totally for some weeks, after which he
L70@P1: returned with profound and difficult solutions to several of them. Jacques Dixmier recalls
L71@P1: Dieudonn´e bounding into a Bourbaki meeting with his usual energy and telling everyone
L72@P1: how a new student had shown up in Nancy with some useless manuscript about integrals
L73@P1: and had earned what Dieudonn´e felt was a well-deserved rebuke – but then had gone off and
L74@P1: solved the bulk of the problems at the end of his recent paper with Schwartz. Dieudonn´e
L75@P1: was frankly impressed, and only too pleased to share his enthusiasm with anyone who

L0@P0: Chapter 4. International Wanderings: 1953-1955
L1@P0: Sao Paulo, 1953-1954 ˜
L2@P0: Faithful to his usual frugal habits, the first thing that Grothendieck did upon arriving
L3@P0: in S˜ao Paulo to take up his new job was to move with his mother into a private house,
L4@P0: and rent himself a piano. The house was situated on rua Oscar Freire, which is now a
L5@P0: chic, modern and central shopping zone; number 1052 where Grothendieck lived is gone,
L6@P0: replaced by a parking lot and a pseudo-chic clothing store.
L7@P0: But the room he had was described by his friends as “tiny”, as all his rooms would
L8@P0: always be: even later on, as a reputed and highly-paid professor, he would continue to
L9@P0: pursue an incongruously modest lifestyle. In 1953, he had good reason to be economical;
L10@P0: although he was receiving a salary, the terms of his contract allowed him to return to Paris
L11@P0: for the entire fall and winter, probably starting in October, when seminars and lecture
L12@P0: courses in France would typically begin. Presumably he was not paid a full salary from
L13@P0: S˜ao Paulo during these months, and in any case, a large proportion of everything he earned
L14@P0: went for the support of Hanka. With the exception of one visit to Brazil, during which
L15@P0: mother and son went up to Rio and spent a few days being taken to all the best tourist
L16@P0: attractions by Paulo Ribenboim and his wife Huguette, Hanka remained in France.
L17@P0: Grothendieck was immediately noticed and made much of by the S˜ao Paulo math
L18@P0: department, which was used to receiving French celebrities and learning the most avantgarde subjects from them, and whose members themselves regularly made the arduous
L19@P0: flight to Paris∗. His reputation preceded him; the department knew all about his six
L20@P0: important publications, each of which could have earned him a doctoral degree, about
L21@P0: the statelessness which prevented him from holding a university position in France, and
L22@P0: about the mother who was dependent on him. Brazil was flourishing economically at that
L23@P0: time, and the department was only too happy to hire the young genius. Chaim H¨onig∗∗,
L24@P0: already a professor at USP, recalls that Grothendieck always remained close to the Paris
L25@P0: mathematical circle, exchanging letters with French mathematicians, keeping abreast of
L26@P0: their work, and hurrying home in the fall to attend as many lectures and seminars as
L27@P0: he could. For his own research, Grothendieck preferred to work at home, and with few

L38@P0-1: 1exceptions, he showed no interest in discussing anything apart from mathematics. He
L39@P1: hardly had any choice in the matter, Professor H¨onig adds: “He had to make his mark
L40@P1: as a mathematician, otherwise his future situation would be extremely complicated”. In
L41@P1: fact, it came as a great surprise to H¨onig when Grothendieck confided to him one day
L42@P1: that as far as a choice of profession was concerned, he hesitated between becoming a
L43@P1: mathematician or a pianist. H¨onig, who had no idea that Grothendieck loved music,
L44@P1: was startled. Although no one seems to remember ever hearing Grothendieck play, he
L45@P1: certainly did play quite regularly (he once claimed to have worked through every single
L46@P1: slow movement of Beethoven’s sonatas), but it does not seem that there could be any
L47@P1: possible comparison between his talent in music and his talent in mathematics.
L48@P1: Still, it was obvious to everyone that outside of the time when Hanka came to visit
L49@P1: S˜ao Paulo in 1953, Grothendieck had no social life at all. In a new alimentary phase
L50@P1: adapted to the continent, he was proud to tell people that he ate nothing but milk, bread
L51@P1: and bananas “so as not to lose any time over it”, and his (lack of) participation in his
L52@P1: colleagues’ cultured conversations revealed the depth of his ignorance of literature, in spite
L53@P1: of his mother’s being, as he always clarified, a writer. He didn’t waste much time chatting
L54@P1: with colleagues anyway, not even about his research.
L55@P1: He did, however, teach; in French, of course, which was understood by everyone in
L56@P1: the mathematical milieu of the time. H¨onig remembers how during one lecture, someone
